Family Health

Cleaning your home for COVID-19: effective routines without unsafe disinfection

Updated: November 4, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A home does not have to be sterile to be cared for well. Regular cleaning removes dirt and many germs; extra disinfection can be useful when someone is ill or has weakened immunity. For COVID-19, a manageable surface routine belongs alongside cleaner air and hand hygiene, rather than endless spraying of everything that enters the house.

Put surface risk in perspective

SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, spreads through respiratory particles released by an infected person, including during breathing and talking. Contaminated hands and surfaces can also contribute, but surface transmission is not the main route. Cleaning a table cannot remove virus-containing particles that people are sharing in poorly ventilated air. Bring in outdoor air safely and use appropriate air filtration where feasible; follow current respiratory precautions when someone is ill.

The often repeated two-to-three-day survival figure comes from an early laboratory experiment on plastic and stainless steel. Conditions, the amount of virus and transfer from a surface to a person all matter. Detecting infectious virus in an experiment does not mean a household object remains equally dangerous for three days, nor that a fixed waiting period makes every item safe. Use sensible cleaning and hygiene rather than a countdown.

Which areas of the home need attention?

Prioritise surfaces people touch often: door and cupboard handles, switches, taps, counters, tables, shared phones, remote controls and keyboards. Include frequently handled car controls if relevant, using the vehicle manufacturer's care advice. Clean these regularly and when dirty; clean less-touched areas as needed. A bag on a table or an outing does not automatically mean that every object needs chemical disinfection.

When someone is sick, add appropriate disinfection after cleaning, especially for shared high-touch surfaces. Extra precautions can also be appropriate for a household member with weakened immunity; agree any specific needs with their care team. Keep food preparation and infant-feeding equipment hygiene suited to their particular task. A general surface disinfectant is not automatically suitable for food, toys that go in a mouth, or feeding items.

Cleaning, sanitising and disinfecting are different

Cleaning uses a suitable detergent or soap, water and physical wiping or scrubbing to remove dirt and many germs. Sanitising lowers germs to levels considered acceptable for a particular public-health use. Disinfecting inactivates or kills specified germs when a suitable product is used correctly. These words are not interchangeable, and none means that a home will stay free of every germ.

Remove visible dirt before disinfection and follow the product's cleaning instructions. Dirt can prevent a disinfectant from working properly. SARS-CoV-2 has a lipid-containing outer envelope that cleaning agents can disrupt, as well as being physically removed during cleaning. Ordinary cleaning is useful; there is no need for antibacterial soap merely because the concern is a virus. A surface that looks clean is not proof of disinfection, but routine cleaning alone is enough in many everyday situations.

Choose the product by its label, not its smell

For disinfection, check that the product is authorised for the intended use where you live, the relevant organism, the surface material and the setting. In the United States, EPA's List N helps identify products expected to work against SARS-CoV-2 when their directions are followed. Match the EPA registration number, rather than relying on a familiar brand name. List inclusion is not a promise that a product suits every surface or is harmless.

Some EPA emerging-virus claims are supported by reviewed evidence against viruses that are harder to inactivate. This is a regulatory route for eligible products, not permission to treat any cleaner advertised against another virus as a coronavirus disinfectant. A claim such as 'kills 99.9%' describes particular test conditions and uses; it cannot guarantee your personal protection. If the label is unclear or unreadable, ask the manufacturer or choose a suitable clearly labelled product.

Use a simple, safe cleaning sequence

Read the directions before starting, keep children and pets away, ventilate the area and wear the gloves or eye protection the label specifies. Clean first, then use the disinfectant only where needed and as directed. Keep the treated surface wet for its stated contact time; wiping it dry immediately may prevent it from working. Follow any rinsing requirement, particularly on food-contact surfaces, and wait until the item is ready for use as directed.

A ready-to-use product does not need extra chemicals added. If dilution is required, follow the actual label exactly; stronger is not necessarily better. Do not mix cleaning products, including bleach with ammonia, acids such as vinegar, or another cleaner. Keep products in their original labelled containers with caps closed and stored securely away from children and pets. Wash your hands after removing cleaning gloves.

Reduce chemical exposure as well as germs

Cleaning and disinfecting products can irritate skin, eyes or airways, and some can trigger asthma. Hazards depend on ingredients, concentration, how a product is used and the exposure. It is misleading to describe every household cleaner as causing cancer, or to assume that a strong smell proves either effectiveness or safety. Bleach and ammonia are not interchangeable descriptions of one type of volatile chemical; mixing products can create dangerous fumes.

Use only the amount and method allowed on the label. Do not spray a person, apply a surface disinfectant to hands or pets, inhale it deliberately, swallow it or put it into food. Do not improvise room fogging or spray clothes while wearing them. If a product causes symptoms, stop the exposure and obtain appropriate advice; someone with asthma or persistent irritation may need another person to clean or a different suitable product.

Clean your hands without substituting surface products

Wash with soap and running water for at least 20 seconds, including fingers, fingertips and the backs of the hands, then dry with a clean towel. Use comfortable lukewarm water rather than very hot water. Important times include after coughing or sneezing, after the toilet, before food preparation or eating, and after handling dirty laundry or cleaning materials. Gloves do not replace handwashing.

If soap and water are unavailable, use a hand sanitiser containing at least 60% alcohol, cover the hands and rub until dry. Wash instead when hands are visibly dirty, greasy or contaminated with chemicals. Do not substitute surface alcohol or disinfectant for a product intended for hands. Supervise children and store sanitiser safely; it can poison someone who swallows it. Both ethanol and isopropanol products can irritate, so do not assume one is always gentler for everyone.

Protect dry or cracked skin

Keep necessary hand hygiene while supporting the skin barrier. Choose a soap your skin tolerates and apply a fragrance-free cream or ointment after washing, while the skin is still slightly damp. Let hand sanitiser dry before moisturising. Repeated wet work, detergents, fragrances and some glove materials can cause irritant or allergic hand dermatitis. Persistent painful cracking, bleeding or a rash deserves clinical advice rather than repeated use of a product that stings.

For cleaning, choose protective gloves suitable for the product and any known allergy. Cotton liners or cotton-lined protective gloves can help with prolonged wet work, but cotton alone is not chemical protection. Keep the inside clean and dry, dry your hands before putting gloves on, and change damp liners. Avoid leaving sweaty gloves on unnecessarily. A clinician can help if eczema or a glove allergy makes routine care difficult.

Follow the device maker's instructions for electronics

Phones, keyboards and remote controls need material-specific care. Turn off and disconnect a device when its instructions require it; use the recommended cloth and avoid liquid entering openings. Do not spray a cleaner directly onto electronics or immerse them. A wipeable cover can make regular cleaning easier if suitable for the device.

Seventy-percent isopropyl alcohol is not a universal screen-cleaning rule. For example, Apple permits certain alcohol wipes on specified hard, nonporous surfaces but has important product and material exceptions. Coatings, leather, fabric and specialist displays can need different care. Check the exact model's guidance before using alcohol or a disinfectant, and do not assume that a product safe for a kitchen counter is safe for a touchscreen.

Laundry and soft furnishings need ordinary care

Wash clothes, towels, bedding and washable cloth toys with detergent at the temperature recommended for the item, and dry them fully. Use the warmest appropriate setting where the care instructions allow it, rather than the hottest setting regardless of material. CDC says a sick person's dirty laundry can be washed with other people's items. Wash hands after handling it and clean the laundry basket as appropriate.

For rugs, upholstery and other soft surfaces, use the care method and product intended for the material; launder or vacuum where appropriate. Do not soak them in a hard-surface disinfectant or assume that alcohol spray replaces washing. A manageable routine that respects materials is more useful than repeatedly applying chemicals to every coat, bag or parcel.

If a cleaning product causes harm

If someone may have swallowed, breathed in or been splashed with a harmful product, seek immediate emergency medical assessment; do not wait for symptoms. If you are unsure whether an exposure is harmful, contact a poison-information service or urgent medical service immediately. After fumes, move to fresh air if you can do so without further exposure. Follow the product's first-aid directions and professional advice for skin or eye contact; do not try to neutralise it with another chemical.

Breathing difficulty, a seizure, fainting or loss of consciousness, or inability to wake requires emergency help now. Do not drive yourself; ask someone to take you or call an ambulance. Do not induce vomiting or give anything to eat or drink while waiting for medical advice about suspected poisoning. Keep the product name or packaging available if safe, without returning to a dangerous area to retrieve it.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Choose a manageable list of high-touch surfaces, improve indoor air where safe and ask the care team about extra precautions for someone with weakened immunity.

Before using a disinfectant, check its intended surface and organism, protection, dilution, wet contact time and rinsing directions; keep chemicals secured and never mix them.

Use the device and fabric care instructions, care for irritated hands, and contact medical or poison services promptly after a potentially harmful exposure.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organise a household cleaning checklist, product names, skin symptoms and questions for a clinician or manufacturer. It cannot verify a disinfectant label, assess chemical exposure, diagnose COVID-19 or guarantee that a surface is safe. Recording information must not delay poison advice or emergency care.

When to seek help

Never mix cleaners or use a surface disinfectant on people, pets or food. Follow the product label and material instructions. Possible harmful swallowing, inhalation or splashes need immediate emergency assessment; uncertainty needs immediate poison-service or urgent medical advice. Breathing difficulty, seizure, fainting or loss of consciousness, or inability to wake is an emergency. Do not drive yourself, induce vomiting or give food or drink while awaiting medical advice about poisoning.

Evidence notes updated: November 4, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Regular cleaning usually suffices; add appropriate disinfection when illness or weakened immunity makes it useful.
  • Prioritise high-touch surfaces while keeping cleaner air and hand hygiene in the plan.
  • Use the actual product label for material, dilution, wet contact time, protection and rinsing; never mix cleaners.
  • Protect hands with appropriate skin care and gloves, and follow device and laundry care instructions.
  • Get immediate advice for possible poisoning; emergency symptoms must not wait for a cleaning task to finish.

Frequently asked questions

How can I reduce coronavirus on surfaces at home?

Clean regularly with a suitable soap or detergent and water, especially high-touch areas. Add a locally authorised disinfectant when someone is ill or has weakened immunity, following the label. Surface care complements cleaner air and hand hygiene.

Which places should I clean first?

Shared handles, switches, taps, tables, counters, phones and controls are sensible priorities. Use material-appropriate methods; there is no need to disinfect every object merely because it came from outside.

Does the virus staying alive for three days mean everything is dangerous?

No. That familiar figure came from early controlled laboratory conditions. It does not measure the chance of infection from your belongings or justify a fixed waiting rule for every object.

Does every disinfectant need the same contact time?

No. Read the actual label and keep the surface wet for that product's specified time. Follow its precleaning, dilution, material and rinsing instructions; an immediate wipe-off may not disinfect.

Can I use 70% alcohol on every phone or screen?

No. Follow the exact device manufacturer's instructions. Some specified hard surfaces tolerate approved alcohol wipes, while coatings and other materials may not. Avoid direct spraying, openings and immersion.

Should I stop washing if my hands become dry?

Keep necessary hygiene and use tolerable soap, lukewarm water and a fragrance-free cream or ointment. Let sanitiser dry before moisturising. Ask a clinician about persistent painful cracks, bleeding or a rash.

Must a sick person's laundry be washed separately on maximum heat?

Not routinely. Use detergent, the recommended temperature and complete drying. CDC permits washing their laundry with other people's items. Follow any specific instructions for a particular infection or care situation.

What should I do after a possible cleaning-product poisoning?

Seek immediate emergency assessment for a possible harmful exposure; if unsure it was harmful, obtain poison-service or urgent medical advice immediately. Breathing difficulty, seizure, fainting or loss of consciousness, or inability to wake is an emergency. Do not drive yourself, induce vomiting, or give food or drink while awaiting medical advice.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
